clue.text: A punishment not quite true, as presented by Carew

parts.note: a rap is a punishment, as in a rap on the knuckles

indicators.note: not quite suggests the word true is slightly out of order, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something presented by the poet Carew is called a penalty that is not entirely truthful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' makes TURE from TRUE. Thomas Carew, a 17th-century Cavalier poet, wrote a poem with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of a Carew poem, so it is the thing the poet presented.

clue.text: Barrister is curious citizen of Warsaw

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or curious
Warsaw is the capital of Poland, so its citizen is a Pole

explanation.surface: A lawyer turns out to be an odd Polish national.
explanation.walkthrough: John Mortimer's fictional barrister, the hero of the TV series Rumpole of the Bailey.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace Rumpole is Mortimer's famous fictional courtroom advocate.

clue.text: One sampling Edgar Allen is a mere versifier

parts.note: the given names of the American writer Poe, so they lead to his surname
someone who samples food or wine is a taster

explanation.surface: Someone reading the works of Edgar Allan Poe is only a minor rhymester.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetaster is a writer of trivial or inferior verse, a mere rhymer.

clue.text: Rabbit fancier

parts.note: reads like a breeder of bunnies, but Rabbit is Harry Angstrom, hero of a series of American novels, and the fancier is the man who created him

explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist who wrote the four Rabbit novels about Harry Angstrom.

explanation.surface: A narrative of the explorer's voyages is said to have two sides to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' rearranges IS DUAL. The epic by Camoens on Vasco da Gama's voyage is known in English as The Lusiad.
explanation.definitionFit: Camoens's Portuguese epic poem tells the story of da Gama's voyage to India.

clue.text: Half-hearted attitude of Hardy's Power Girl

explanation.surface: A literary heroine of Hardy's shows only lukewarm commitment.
explanation.walkthrough: Paula Power is the heroine of Hardy's novel A Laodicean, and a Laodicean is a person indifferent in religion or politics.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean tepid and indifferent: half-hearted feeling, and the Laodicean indifference that gives Paula Power's novel its title.

clue.text: "And clearest —, amplitude of mind" (Wordsworth)

parts.note: a line from Wordsworth's Prelude with one word missing, the clear perception paired with breadth of mind

explanation.surface: A line of Wordsworth's verse with a gap to fill.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word of the line, meaning deep understanding or perception.

clue.text: Degas subjects in French and English purposes

parts.note: dans is the French word for in
uses are purposes, as in what something is for

explanation.surface: The painter's subjects are described in a mixture of French and English terms.
explanation.definitionFit: Female ballet dancers were the favourite subjects of the painter Degas.

clue.text: Threatens rascal at the finish

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child or rascal
the end is the finish

explanation.surface: A scoundrel issues threats at the very last moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that impends looms over or menaces, as danger hangs over someone.

clue.text: Defenceless child heard described by Asimov and Ted Willis

parts.note: naked can mean unprotected or defenceless

indicators.note: heard says the word for a child is to be taken by its sound

parts.note: a son is a child

explanation.surface: An unprotected infant is the subject of works by two writers.
explanation.walkthrough: Asimov's robot novel and a play by Ted Willis share the title The Naked Sun.
explanation.definitionFit: The title shared by an Asimov novel and a Ted Willis play, so both writers described it.

clue.text: Ask Maori about Greek dances

indicators.note: about here signals that the letters of ask Maori are moved around

explanation.surface: Someone asks a New Zealander about traditional Greek folk dances.
explanation.definitionFit: The romaika is a traditional Greek folk dance.

clue.text: "His tail -d more / Even than before " (Ingoldsby Legends)

parts.words: "His tail -d more / Even than before " (Ingoldsby Legends)
parts.note: a couplet from the Ingoldsby Legends with a verb missing; the '-d' shows the missing word takes a past-tense ending

explanation.surface: A couplet from comic Victorian verse about a creature's tail, with a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ingoldsby Legends are comic Victorian verse tales by Richard Barham; the jackdaw's tail moved more than ever.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb, meaning to shake or move from side to side.

clue.text: Like Graham Greene's man and Edward Thomas's muse

definitions.text: Like Graham Greene's man and Edward Thomas's muse

parts.words: Like Graham Greene's man and Edward Thomas's muse
parts.note: Greene wrote a novel about a man chosen by lot as the one in ten, and Thomas wrote a poem naming the muse who follows the nine

explanation.definitionFit: The ordinal shared by the titles The Tenth Man by Greene and The Tenth Muse by Thomas.

clue.text: He of the breathing flute and sounding lyre, as reported by Dryden

parts.words: He of the breathing flute and sounding lyre, as reported by Dryden
parts.note: describes the musician who plays for Alexander the Great in Dryden's ode Alexander's Feast

explanation.definitionFit: The court musician of Alexander the Great, whose flute and lyre Dryden celebrates in Alexander's Feast.

clue.text: Slanderous troublemaker, sits there, stirring it up

indicators.note: stirring it up says the letters of sits there are mixed together

explanation.surface: A scandalmonger sits there, causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirring it up' rearranges SITS THERE. The character is the foul-mouthed Greek soldier in Homer's Iliad and Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida.
explanation.definitionFit: The railing Greek soldier who abuses his leaders in the Iliad, a byword for a scurrilous carper.

clue.text: John Dennis's sort of reviewer

parts.note: the critic John Dennis wrote a 1693 work about a fair-minded critic

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective in the title of Dennis's The Impartial Critick, meaning unbiased.

clue.text: Lands the new edition of Henri Beyle

indicators.note: a new edition reissues the words lands the in a changed form, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A publisher secures the latest edition of a French author's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new edition of' rearranges LANDS THE. Henri Beyle was the real name of the French novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name of Henri Beyle, author of Le Rouge et le Noir.

clue.text: Cutting instrument produces very small book ?

parts.note: micro means very small
a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: A tiny volume turns out to be a sharp tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A microtome is an instrument for slicing very thin sections for microscopy.

clue.text: Wise old teacher, now recognized as a high flyer

definitions.text: now recognized as a high flyer

explanation.surface: A sage once tutoring heroes is now known to be soaring.
explanation.walkthrough: The wise centaur tutored Achilles and others; in 1977 a small body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus was given his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The centaur who tutored Greek heroes, and the minor planet in the outer solar system named after him.

clue.text: Dubious types may start selling pamphlets in Victorian style

explanation.surface: Shady characters might begin hawking tracts in a nineteenth-century manner.

clue.text: A Madeleine with a past predating Proust

parts.note: reads like Proust's famous cake that brings back memories, but it is the alias Monsieur Madeleine of the ex-convict in Hugo's Les Misérables

clue.text: "To dine with Lord Lobster " (and count W. H. Auden)

parts.words: "To dine with Lord Lobster " (and count W. H. Auden)
parts.note: a quotation completed by naming the condition behind a refusal, with Auden counted among those who suffered it

clue.text: The curse on ancient Greek citizen

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek is placed under a curse.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of Thebes, the ancient Greek city.

clue.text: "With the blast of thy the waters were gathered together " (Exodus)

parts.words: "With the blast of thy the waters were gathered together " (Exodus)
parts.note: a verse from the Song of Moses with one word missing, the breath of God piling up the sea

clue.text: Bronte character studiously learns Hawthorne (but not entirely)

indicators.note: but not entirely says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A Bronte character studies the American novelist Hawthorne, though only partly.

clue.text: In high places early in his career, he later reached overload

parts.note: In High Places and Overload are titles by the same bestselling novelist, the first earlier and the second later

explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Hailey, the Anglo-Canadian novelist who wrote In High Places (1962) and Overload (1979).

clue.text: That of Felix's drayhorse was bright and battering

parts.words: That of Felix's drayhorse was bright and battering
parts.note: a description of the shining heavy shoe worn by the great carthorse in a poem about the blacksmith Felix

explanation.definitionFit: In Hopkins's Felix Randal the blacksmith fettles the great drayhorse its bright and battering sandal, a horseshoe.

clue.text: Pulitzer prizewinner's young horse a long time on the heather

parts.note: a year is a long period of time
ling is another name for common heather

explanation.surface: A prize-winning author's colt spends ages out on the moor.
explanation.walkthrough: Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings won the Pulitzer Prize for The Yearling, though her young animal is a fawn.
